system_prompt:
You are a voice assistant. You are speaking out loud to one person, in a conversation.

Your replies are converted to speech, so:
- Answer in one or two spoken sentences. Never use bullet points, numbered lists, headings, or markdown of any kind.
- Never read out code, file paths, or URLs unless you are explicitly asked for one.
- Do not restate the question before answering it.
- Do not narrate what you are about to do. Just do it, then say what happened.
- If you do not know something, say so in one sentence rather than guessing at length.

You are helping with software work on the user's machine. You have access to
tools for reading files, searching the codebase, and looking things up. Prefer
answering from what you already know; reach for a tool only when the answer
genuinely depends on something you cannot know without one.

The user is talking to you while doing something else. Brevity is not a style
preference here, it is the whole job: a reply that takes twenty seconds to speak
is a reply they will interrupt. Say the useful part first.

When you throw a question or image at a vector database, the first thing that happens is some model turns that input into a list of numbers, essentially a fingerprint of its meaning. The database has already done this for every item in its collection, so it has a huge pile of these numeric fingerprints waiting. It then compares your fingerprint against those stored ones, usually measuring how much the numbers overlap or how close they are in some mathematical space, and returns whichever items land closest to yours. The clever part is that this "closeness" has nothing to do with exact matching; it captures semantic similarity, so a query about "cars that go fast" can match an article titled "supercars break records" even though no words overlap at all. That's what makes it so useful. You can search through millions of documents, images, or audio clips in milliseconds, build recommendations that actually understand what people mean rather than just what they clicked on before, power chatbots that ground their answers in a company's private knowledge, or find near-duplicate content across a huge corpus. Where a traditional database asks "does this value equal that value," a vector database asks "does this thing resemble that thing," and that single shift opens up search, recommendation, and retrieval problems that were basically intractable before.

A vector database works by turning everything it stores into long lists of numbers, or embeddings, which are produced by a model trained to place semantically similar things close together in that number space. A photo, a sentence, a product, a chunk of text, or a piece of audio can all become a vector, and two vectors that describe similar things end up with similar numbers. When you search, you convert your query into a vector the same way and then the database finds the stored vectors whose numbers are closest, usually measuring closeness with something like cosine similarity or dot product. Instead of matching exact words, it matches meaning. That is what makes it useful. You can search for documents that say the same thing in different words, recommend products that match how a customer described a need they cannot name precisely, deduplicate photos and audio, feed a language model only the most relevant context before it answers, or let a person search a library by describing what they vaguely remember. It also works across modalities, so a sentence can find an image or a product can find a review, because the model placed them in a shared space where "closeness" means "relatedness."

A vector database works by turning whatever you want to search—text, images, audio, or even code—into a long list of numbers called an embedding or vector. Each item gets its own vector, and the model that creates these vectors has a special property: things that are similar in meaning end up close together in this high-dimensional space, while unrelated things land far apart. So "a dog chasing a ball" and "puppy runs after tennis ball" produce vectors that sit nearly on top of each other, while "quarterly financial report" lands way over there, even though the words are completely different.

When you ask a query, the database converts your question into a vector using the same model, then runs a nearest-neighbor search to find the stored vectors with the smallest distance—usually measured by cosine similarity or dot product. Finding the closest point in thousands of dimensions is expensive, so most vector databases use clever indexing tricks like HNSW graphs, which build layers of skip-list-like structures that let you hop around the space quickly, or product quantization, which compresses vectors into smaller codes and scans them in batches.

This is useful because it sidesteps the brittleness of keyword matching. "How do I make my app faster" can find documents about caching, profiling, and lazy loading without those words ever appearing in the query. It powers retrieval-augmented generation for large language models, lets you build "find similar products" features, powers semantic search, deduplication, recommendation systems, and anomaly detection. In short, it turns "vibes and meaning" into geometry, and geometry is something you can search really fast.

A vector database works by turning whatever you throw at it—a sentence, an image, a song, a product description—into a long list of numbers. That list is the vector, and it captures meaning rather than surface details. Two things that mean roughly the same end up with vectors that sit close together in this high-dimensional space, while unrelated things land far apart. When you ask it to find similar items, it doesn't scan every row and compare strings the way a traditional database does. Instead it takes your query, converts it into a vector, and then hunts through an index—usually a clever structure like a graph or a tree—that lets it jump straight to the neighborhood of closest vectors instead of checking all of them. That's why it stays fast even with millions of entries. The usefulness is that similarity becomes a matter of geometry instead of vocabulary. You can search a codebase for the function that does what you describe without knowing its name, match a new photo to a similar one even if the subjects differ in pose, or let a language model pull in the right background facts before it answers a question. In other words, it turns "find me things like this" from a fuzzy, keyword-dependent mess into a precise, scalable computation, and that single shift is what powers a lot of modern search, recommendation, and retrieval-augmented AI systems.

A vector database starts by taking whatever you want to store—words, pictures, sound—and pushing it through a neural network that spits out a long list of numbers. That list is the embedding, and each number roughly captures one facet of the item's meaning. The database's whole trick is that similar items end up with similar numbers, so "king" and "queen" sit close together in that number space even though they share no characters. When you come in with a query, the database runs it through the same model, gets its own list of numbers, and then does a nearest-neighbor search: it walks through its stored lists and ranks them by how close they are to yours, usually measured by cosine similarity or distance in Euclidean space. For speed it doesn't compare against every single vector; it uses an approximate algorithm like HNSW that builds a graph of neighbors and hops through it, which is why the "A" in ANN keeps showing up. Why does this matter? Because similarity in meaning is exactly what keyword matching misses. Search that understands "fast car" matches "speedy automobile," image search finds pictures by concept instead of filename, recommendation systems connect users to things they actually resemble, and duplicate detection spots near-identical records in messy data. In short, it turns fuzzy human notions of resemblance into a number-crunching problem a computer can answer in milliseconds.

A vector database works by taking each piece of data you hand it — a document, an image, a product description, whatever — and running it through a model that produces a long list of numbers, called an embedding or a vector. That list of numbers is a kind of compressed description of what the data means, not what it says. Two items with similar meaning end up with vectors that land close together in a high-dimensional space, and two items that are unrelated land far apart.

When you later ask for similar items, the database does the same thing to your query, turning it into a vector, and then finds the stored vectors that are geometrically closest to it. It uses clever indexing tricks, like approximating nearest-neighbor search, to do this fast even across billions of vectors instead of comparing your query against every single one, which would be far too slow.

The usefulness is that it lets you search by meaning rather than by exact words. A person looking for a red running shoe that's good on wet trails won't type the exact marketing copy, but their query's vector still lands near matching products. It powers semantic search, recommendation systems, image search, "find similar" features, and a lot of the retrieval step behind large language model applications, where relevant context is pulled from a corpus before being handed to the model.

A vector database works by turning everything you throw at it into a list of numbers, what people call an embedding. Text, images, audio, whatever you have, gets run through a model that outputs a long vector where the meaning of the thing is encoded in the positions and values of those numbers. Similar things end up close together in this high-dimensional space, and dissimilar things end up far apart. So when you want to find similar items, you take your query, convert it to a vector the same way, and then the database hunts through its stored vectors looking for the ones that sit closest to yours, usually measured by something like cosine similarity or distance in the space. Modern databases use clever indexing tricks like approximate nearest neighbor search so they don't have to check every single stored vector one by one, which would be way too slow past a few thousand items. The usefulness comes from the fact that "similarity" in vector space captures meaning, not just matching keywords. A search for "happy puppy" can find a document that says "cheerful dog" even though they share almost no words. That's why it's so powerful for semantic search, recommendation systems, deduplication, finding near-duplicate content, and powering the retrieval layer in large language model applications where you need to pull relevant context for a question.

When a vector database goes looking for similar items, it's really just doing a kind of geometric matching in a high-dimensional space. When something comes in that you want to store or search for, the system first converts it into a vector, which is a long list of numbers that captures the essence of that item. notes: Assembled from six probe runs on the same machine against the same resident model. Every case and every sample records the run it came from in its `run` field, and `runs` lists each run with its command.

prefill-cold-6000 is INVALID and is kept rather than quietly dropped: the padding overran num_ctx 8192, Ollama truncated the prompt to ~4098 tokens, and the truncated prompt then matched the previous case, so the row reports a cache hit instead of a 6000-token prefill. prefill-cold-3000 is the largest valid cold point.

prompt_eval_count reports the whole prompt whether or not Ollama had to evaluate it. prefill_tok_per_s on a cache-hit row (cache-exact-repeat, and the invalid 6000 rows) is therefore a full token count divided by a near-zero duration, not a throughput measurement.

The probe builds its own system prompt and tool block rather than assembling the real persona, landing at ~1195 prompt tokens against the product path's ~1654. Its absolute numbers accordingly run a little below the product-path numbers quoted in the results doc.
n=5 per case. Five samples separate 4.4 s from 0.6 s with room to spare and cannot resolve a 15 percent difference; no claim in the results doc rests on one.

The gate flags in each case summary are the criteria doc's fix gate (p50 first content <= 1500 ms, no <think> in content, every sample answered). Diagnostic cases are expected to fail it; failing is what makes them diagnostic.
